deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT (from pp. 28 and 30). alpha(x,y,z) is a harmonic potential. Its gradient is (p,q,r) = (alpha_x, alpha_y, alpha_z), so curl(p,q,r)=0 and p_x+q_y+r_z=0. The modulus m = p^2+q^2(+r^2) is assumed to be a function of alpha alone. This is the condition for a temperature to depend only on time and the single variable alpha (an isoparametric family). Riemann sorts cases by how many of p,q,r are functionally independent. Case 1 (three independent, p.28) gives concentric spheres. This page treats Case 2: one relation r = r(p,q), free of x,y,z.

STEP 1. From p.28, put a = r_p, b = r_q, with a_q = b_p. The top line r_x = a p_x (+ b q_x) is a carried-over fragment. Use curl-freeness (r_x = p_z, r_y = q_z, q_x = p_y). Then p_z = a p_x + b p_y, q_z = a q_x + b q_y and r_z = a r_x + b r_y. Hence every function F(p,q,r) satisfies F_z = a F_x + b F_y.

STEP 2. Unless (8) p^2+q^2+r^2 = const holds, alpha depends on the same two variables as p,q,r, i.e. alpha = alpha(p,q). [Implicit, mine: m is a function of alpha and not constant, so alpha is a function of m, hence of p,q.] Applying STEP 1 to F = alpha gives r = alpha_z = a p + b q. So r is homogeneous of degree 1 in (p,q) (Euler). Differentiating r = a p + b q gives p a_p + q b_p = 0 and p a_q + q b_q = 0. Hence (8'): a_p b_q - b_p a_q = 0. The Hessian of r vanishes, so the surface r = r(p,q) is developable (a cone through the origin).

STEP 3 (Legendre transform). Put s = alpha - x p - y q - z r. Then ds = -x dp - y dq - z dr = -(x + a z) dp - (y + b z) dq. So s = s(p,q), and (9): s_p = -x - a z, s_q = -y - b z.

STEP 4. Rewrite the divergence equation using (p,q,z) as independent variables. Let J = p_x q_y - p_y q_x. Then x_p = q_y/J, x_q = -p_y/J, y_p = -q_x/J, y_q = p_x/J. Also p_z = -J(y_q x_z - x_q y_z) and q_z = -J(x_p y_z - y_p x_z). Dividing by J gives
x_p + y_q - a(y_q x_z - x_q y_z) - b(x_p y_z - y_p x_z) = 0.
By (9), x_z = -a, y_z = -b, x_p = -s_pp - a_p z, y_q = -s_qq - b_q z, x_q = -s_pq - a_q z, y_p = -s_pq - b_p z. Up to an overall sign the equation becomes
z{(1+b^2)a_p - ab(a_q+b_p) + (1+a^2)b_q} + (1+b^2)s_pp - 2ab s_pq + (1+a^2)s_qq = 0.
Since a, b, s do not depend on z, this splits into (10) and (11):
(10) (1+b^2)s_pp - 2ab s_pq + (1+a^2)s_qq = 0.
(11) (1+r_q^2)r_pp - 2 r_p r_q r_pq + (1+r_p^2)r_qq = 0.

STEP 5. Equation (11) is the minimal-surface equation for the graph r = r(p,q) in (p,q,r)-space. By (8) or (8') this surface is also a sphere or a developable surface. A sphere is not minimal, and a developable minimal surface (K=0, H=0) is a plane. So the surface is a plane through the origin and a, b are constants. Rotating the z-axis makes a = b = 0, i.e. r = 0, so alpha is independent of z.

STEP 6. Equation (10) becomes s_pp + s_qq = 0. [Implicit, mine: s - p s_p - q s_q = alpha = f(m). Its general solution is a particular solution psi(m), with psi - 2m psi' = f, plus a degree-1 homogeneous part.] This gives s = psi(m) + p chi(beta), with m = p^2+q^2 and beta = q/p. Then
-x = s_p = 2p psi'(m) + chi(beta) - beta chi'(beta),
-y = s_q = 2q psi'(m) + chi'(beta).
The margin computation gives s_pp = 2psi' + 4p^2 psi'' + beta^2 chi''/p and s_qq = 2psi' + 4q^2 psi'' + chi''/p. Hence s_pp + s_qq = 4psi' + 4m psi'' + (1+beta^2) chi''/p. With p = sqrt(m)/sqrt(1+beta^2) this gives sqrt(m)(4psi' + 4m psi'') + (1+beta^2)^(3/2) chi''(beta) = 0. Since m and beta are independent, it separates:
sqrt(m)(4psi' + 4m psi'') = k, chi'' = -k/(1+beta^2)^(3/2).
The page writes +k in the second equation. 

STEP 7 (continued on p.30). Integrating gives chi = k sqrt(1+beta^2) + const + const*beta. Then x + a = -(2 sqrt(m) psi' + k)/sqrt(1+beta^2) and y + b = beta*(same). So (x+a)^2 + (y+b)^2 is a function of m, hence of alpha. The isothermal surfaces are coaxial circular cylinders.
errors: Sign slip in the separation: from sqrt(m)(4psi'+4m psi'') + (1+beta^2)^(3/2) chi'' = 0 and sqrt(m)(4psi'+4m psi'') = k it follows that chi'' = -k/(1+beta^2)^(3/2), not +k. The slip propagates to p.30 (chi = +k sqrt(1+beta^2), x+a = -(2sqrt(m)psi'+k)/sqrt(1+beta^2)). It is harmless for the geometric conclusion (coaxial cylinders), but the constant k in the psi-ODE and in the cylinder radius then differ in sign.
Implicit step: the ansatz s = psi(m) + p chi(q/p) is not justified on the page ('ut in casu primo'). It follows from s - p s_p - q s_q = alpha = f(m), with degree-1 homogeneous solutions p chi(q/p).
Implicit step: concluding alpha = alpha(p,q) uses the standing hypothesis that m is a function of alpha and m is non-constant. This is not restated on the page.
Minor: the overall sign of the transformed divergence equation is flipped relative to direct substitution. This is irrelevant since it equals 0.
Minor: the division by p and the substitution p = sqrt(m)/sqrt(1+beta^2) assume p > 0. The case p = 0 is not treated separately.
Notation clash: a, b first denote r_p, r_q and later (p.30) arbitrary integration constants.
'Minimal + developable implies plane' is asserted without proof. It is true (H=0 and K=0 force both principal curvatures to vanish).

results.what: In case 2 (one relation r=r(p,q) among the gradient components), r is homogeneous of degree 1, so the gradient-image surface is a cone and its Hessian vanishes (8').
results.modern_name: Euler homogeneity / developability of the gradient image

results.what: Legendre transform s = alpha - x p - y q - z r of the potential, used to linearize the problem in gradient (hodograph) variables.
Div(grad alpha)=0 in hodograph variables (p,q,z) splits into a minimal-surface equation for r(p,q) and a linear second-order equation for s.
results.modern_name: Hodograph form of the Laplace equation; the minimal surface equation appears as the gradient-image condition

results.what: Classification of harmonic potentials with |grad alpha| a function of alpha (equivalently, isoparametric families in R^3 / temperatures depending on time and one variable). Level sets are parallel planes, concentric spheres or coaxial cylinders; this page proves the cylinder case and excludes the sphere case.
results.modern_name: Classification of isoparametric surfaces in Euclidean 3-space
results.usually_credited_to: Laura (1918), Somigliana (1919), Levi-Civita (1937), B. Segre (1938, R^n); Lamé earlier on isothermal surfaces

results.what: Separation sqrt(m)(4psi'+4m psi'') = k, chi''=±k/(1+beta^2)^(3/2), solved explicitly to give cylinders.
results.modern_name: Separation of variables in polar form of the 2D Laplace equation for the Legendre transform

deep.surprise_reason: The page belongs to a complete case analysis (spheres, cylinders, planes) of when a temperature can depend on time and one spatial variable. In modern terms this is the classification of isoparametric families in R^3. It is usually attributed to Laura/Somigliana (1918-19) and Levi-Civita/Segre (1937-38). Riemann's proof via the Legendre transform, with minimal surfaces in gradient space, is elegant and non-routine. However, the R^3 statement was probably accessible earlier (Lamé's school), and the material may be partly known from Riemann's heat-conduction Nachlass (related to the 1861 Paris memoir). Hence notable but not a major priority shift.

checkable.asserts: Laplacian in (p,q) of s = psi(m) + p chi(q/p) equals 4psi' + 4m psi'' + (1+beta^2) chi''/p (should be 0).
chi = k sqrt(1+beta^2) has chi'' = +k/(1+beta^2)^(3/2), consistent with the page's (sign-slipped) equation (=0).

checkable.sympy: b,k,c1,c2=symbols('beta k c1 c2'); chi=k*sqrt(1+b**2)+c1+c2*b; simplify(chi - b*diff(chi,b) - (k/sqrt(1+b**2)+c1))
checkable.asserts: chi - beta chi' = k/sqrt(1+beta^2) + const, giving -x - a = (2 sqrt(m) psi' + k)/sqrt(1+beta^2) (=0).
